title: Beyond the Weekend: Building Confidence With Implant Mentorship
html:
Ongoing clinical support can help dentists translate education into successful implementation.

By Brad Millard, DDS November 1, 2026 Volume 22 , Issue 8 , November/December 2026 Page(s): 10

Share

If you’ve taken a weekend dental course, you know this feeling. You spend long days absorbing lectures, going through hands-on exercises, and leaving with a guide full of protocols. You leave the course, and you’re ready. Then you go back to your practice; a real patient sits down in your chair, and their case doesn’t quite match the one in the binder. Now what? You try to think about the techniques and everything you learned, but in the back of your mind you can’t shake the thought that it would be really helpful to bounce this case off of someone else.

This feeling isn’t the fault of the individual dentist, but rather a structural gap in how these courses have traditionally been taught. It’s also, I believe, one of the biggest reasons clinicians are hesitant to add implants to their practice, even after completing the coursework.

Over the past decade, implant dentistry has grown into a service that nearly every general practice is expected to offer, and educational programs are starting to recognize that training and confidence do not go hand in hand, and that closing the gap between them requires more than a weekend.

Traditional Weekend Courses

Continuing education for dentists has typically fallen into two tracks. The first and most common is the traditional weekend course. These courses are typically centered on a specific product or system, intended to help clinicians feel comfortable with a new product and begin using it in their practice. The course delivers exactly what it is intended to: here is a product, here are the capabilities, here is a guide to how to use it day-to-day. This style shouldn’t be completely dismissed, as it can be a solid foundation for understanding a new procedure, but it lacks depth and tends to end just as clinical practice becomes more complex.

While dentists may learn new techniques during weekend training, they are unlikely to be fully prepared to make judgment calls when an actual patient is right in front of them. What happens when their anatomy doesn’t perfectly match the textbook, or they have a complicated medical history that raises multiple questions, or when something goes sideways mid-procedure? It’s easy to leave the weekend with the knowledge of “how,” but not necessarily the answers to “what if.” They have to find these answers for themselves, and it can feel daunting and isolating.

Where Mentorship-Based Training Comes In

This is where the second type of continuing education comes in. Mentor-based training programs are gaining industrywide traction. Rather than viewing the weekend course as the end of the program, mentorship models view these sessions as the starting point for a long relationship. They still focus on didactic learning and hands-on experiences. But they also have clinical experience with models and then with live patients, with an experienced clinician right next to you before you go back to your practice. And once the course has ended, you have continued access to the community of mentors.

Many mentor-based implant dentistry courses also tend to differentiate themselves by being open and honest about complications. Most courses market themselves with success stories, but real implant dentistry includes cases that don’t always go smoothly. A course that takes the time to acknowledge what can go wrong and how to manage it gives dentists more confidence as they move forward.

It’s easy to see why this type of education is more appealing. Having a support system to rely on is paramount to building confidence in a new skill, especially because dentistry involving live patients rarely goes according to plan. It can turn the idea of “I hope this goes well” to “I know who to turn to if I have questions.”

Team Training is Important

While individual readiness might be one obstacle a general dentist needs to overcome, another is getting their team on board. A dentist can leave a weekend course with full confidence and excitement about placing implants, but they lose steam once their staff starts questioning this new procedure. It’s not because they doubt the dentist, but rather because they feel left in the dark about it. Hygienists, assistants, and even front-desk staff are now expected to support a procedure they don’t understand, which creates hesitation.

Strong mentorship-based programs also offer educational programs for the entire staff, not just the dentist. When the staff understands what is happening, why it’s happening, and their individual roles, there’s buy-in rather than pushback. Now, there’s a team that’s invested in the success of implementing the new procedure.

Mentorship in Practice

What sets mentorship-based programs apart from other courses is what happens after the course ends. The best programs offer real-time guidance and access to a community of other dentists, whether through a forum, a direct line to a mentor, or the opportunity for an experienced clinician to assist in the first few cases. That community support makes all the difference in the success of adding implant dentistry to a practice.

A case that comes to mind is when a newer clinician was evaluating a moderate-complexity implant case in the anterior esthetic zone for a 32-year-old patient. One question changed the entire outcome of the case: “How’s her smile line?” He noted that she had a high smile line and then paused for a moment; he hadn’t considered that a high smile line meant that any imperfection in the restoration would likely be visible when she smiled. That single question and the thoughts that followed were enough to prompt this clinician to refer to a periodontist. The periodontist recommended soft-tissue grafting before the implant placement to improve the esthetic result. Without that conversation the case would have been a straightforward and successful implant placement, but the overall esthetic outcome would have been different from what the patient needed or wanted.

This case shows the value of mentorship. The mentor didn’t step in to fix a mistake; instead, they asked simple questions that a newer clinician hadn’t thought to ask before a mistake could become a problem.

What to Look for in an Implant Education Program

Dentists looking for training programs have many options. When trying to distinguish between a program that is built for long-term success from one that is built on sales, there are a few things to consider:

  • Does this course address complications honestly? A course that only shows successful outcomes isn’t showing the whole picture.
  • Is there a clear path from learning to doing? Look for a course that offers lecture, hands-on experience, and live-patient work.
  • Is my team included? Full team training leads to a higher practice-wide implementation.
  • What happens when the course ends? A course that offers a forum or direct access to a mentor provides guidance for ongoing success.
  • Is it sales-driven? Be cautious of programs that boast guarantees or focus on the product rather than the clinician.

If a program seems too easy, too cheap, or too good to be true, it probably is.

Building Confidence and Predictable Outcomes

Predictable outcomes come from having a system, not just hoping for a good day. A good restaurant doesn’t succeed because the chef is talented. It succeeds because there is a process behind the scenes, from specific ingredients and timing to a well-thought-out recipe; put these together, and you get a known result every time. Implant dentistry works the same way. The training program provides the dentist with a protocol to follow and a mentor to guide them. When this happens, guesswork is replaced by repeatable, confident, and predictable cases.

The Path Forward

Weekend courses are still a valuable starting point for growth in dentistry, but education that ends on the weekend leaves dentists and their patients vulnerable. Mentorship-based models are what actually build clinical confidence and successful implementation.

It’s worth considering the familiar observation that doing the same thing repeatedly while expecting a different result is unlikely to produce change. Dentists who have taken course after course only to fail at the implementation stage, and who might be thinking about which course to try next, should be asking why the format itself isn’t sticking. Usually it’s not individual ability, but rather the lack of support.

As the offering of implant dentistry in general practices continues to grow, dentists should consider finding a program that supports them on day 1 and day 100.
